Inside Rosie Dart’s London Home Full of Clever Storage and Vintage Character

Inside Rosie Dart’s London Home Full of Clever Storage and Vintage Character

Content creator Rosie Dart believes character matters more than square metres. See how she transformed a blank-canvas West London apartment with a bespoke double-height storage wall, vintage finds and a playful approach to colour.
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 1:16
Instaread

When Rosie Dart first moved into her apartment, it felt more like a shell than a home. There was little built-in storage, few original details and an abundance of sad white walls waiting for direction. Layer by layer, Rosie introduced hardworking joinery, carefully chosen vintage pieces and a rich palette of colour to craft a home that feels both deeply personal and quietly practical.

Rosie spent years working in film and television before turning her attention to content creation, directing and design. She has also long been inspired by director Wes Anderson and his approach to “world building”. All of this, has helped to hone the cinematic eye that guided her approach to designing and styling her home. Every object has been chosen with intention. Every room has its own atmosphere. Instead of filling the apartment with furniture, Rosie edits what stays, giving each piece space to contribute to the overall story of her home.

An Entrance That Creates a Sense of Arrival

Rosie introduced a movable storage unit by the front door to create a small entrance sequence and to make the arrival into the living room feel less abrupt. Shoes can slot in beneath the unit, everyday essentials can be easily dumped and organised here, and the apartment immediately feels more considered from the outset. 

This same thinking continues throughout. When Rosie moved in there was almost no built-in storage, so she gradually introduced joinery wherever it was needed. Rather than adding more furniture, she built places for everyday objects to be stored away, allowing the things she loves most to be on display and become a focal point instead.

One Wall That Changes Everything

The apartment's biggest transformation took place across a single wall. Rosie “wanted to make the most of the vertical space” available to her and so designed a floor-to-ceiling plywood shelving system that now stores, displays and organises much of her home. Working with a local plywood joinery studio, Lozi, Rosie refined every detail until the shelving unit felt as practical as it was beautiful. A bank of cupboards ground the base of the unit – providing generous storage for all the things Rosie likes to keep hidden away – and open shelving sits on top for displaying all of Rosie’s “decorative pieces”. Working with the expert team at Lozi meant they were able to help in refining Rosie’s design. For instance, they suggested adding little notches to the rear of each of the shelves to corral cables allowing Rosie to “have loads of lamps and atmospheric lighting” within the unit.

A sliding library ladder, also in plywood, makes every shelf accessible, even those closest to the ceiling, which are ingeniously recessed slightly as Rosie didn’t want the top of the unit to “feel too bulky or looming”. A thriving collection of indoor plants lines the top of the shelving unit, which was Rosie’s device for livening up “the strip of wall” that was exposed at the top where the unit ended. 

Beneath the living room window, a mustard-toned Togo sofa shares the space with a DIY glass-brick coffee table that Rosie loves for the way it catches and diffuses the afternoon light and opposite a gallery wall minimises the visual heaviness of the wall-mounted television.

A Kitchen That Finds Storage Everywhere

The original kitchen wasn't short of cupboards. It simply wasn't using them well. Rather than starting again, Rosie reworked almost every element to make the space more efficient. Birch plywood cabinetry brings warmth and continuity with the rest of the apartment’s joinery, while open shelving replaces bulky upper cupboards, making the kitchen feel more generous. 

Every inch has been maximised for efficiency and to suit Rosie’s needs: a wine rack has been replaced with a “mini larder” and wine glasses are suspended by custom slits in one the shelves. Even the narrow gap beneath the oven has become a slim drawer for baking trays and supplies. The room also carries Rosie's playful approach to materials and colour, this time with a “Americana 50s diner-inspired look”. Leftover bathroom tiles were preserved and spray-painted by Rosie to create a blue-white checkerboard splashback and concealed strip lighting brings a soft glow to the kitchen at night. Between the kitchen and living room, a custom extendable dining table bridges the spaces, making it just as suited to hosting friends as it is to everyday meals.

A Home That Changes With Colour

Walk into the lower-level bedroom and surprisingly, it’s filled with light from two generous windows and Rosie’s colour-drenched the space in a soft green to enhance its sense of calm. A gamble was taken to rip up the existing grey carpet – one that was rewarded with original Victorian floorboards. To make the most of a shallow recess not quite deep enough for a wardrobe, Rosie has installed hanging rails designed by our friend Simone Giertz at Yetch Studio that include clever integrated coat “hingers” that fold in half.  

Butter yellow is the hero colour of Rosie’s bathroom and Wes Anderson was her muse. Rosie resisted the temptation to replace the bath with a standalone shower, choosing instead to preserve the ritual of slowing down at the end of the day. A striking blue concrete basin was added to add interest and personality to the space.

Living Vertically

The apartment's greatest luxury isn't extra floor space, it's height. Rosie uses the mezzanine as a room that changes throughout the day and also contains bulk storage. In the morning, a desk slides out from beneath custom joinery at the foot of a guest bed to create a dedicated workspace overlooking her living room. When work is finished, the desk unit slides neatly away again. 

Raising the bed created enough space for more cupboards below and above the bed, a pegboard keeps everyday tools within reach. Two other small storage units designed specifically for the space tidy away and store bulky items such as luggage, a drying rack, Rosie's printer and her art and supplies.

"Living in a small space really makes you think about your possessions. I love collecting objects and antiques, but because I have a finite amount of room, it really helps me curate and ensure that every piece feels intentional and has a home."
